Anterior Cruciate Ligament
Out-of-Laboratory Longitudinal Gait Assessment of
Participants Before and After Anterior Cruciate
Ligament Reconstruction Surgery: An Observational
Longitudinal Study
Tomer Yona, PhD*; Bezalel Peskin, MD†; Arielle G. Fischer, PhD*
*Technion, Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa; †Rambam Medical Center, Haifa, Israel
Background: After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruc-
tion (ACLR), individuals often demonstrate altered knee kine-
matics during walking. Understanding these changes across
recovery time points is important for informing rehabilitation
and return-to-sport decisions.
Objectives: To evaluate the longitudinal changes in knee
sagittal-plane kinematics before and after ACLR during varying
walking speeds in nonlaboratory environments and to describe
hip- and ankle-joint kinematics.
Design: Observational longitudinal study.
Setting: Hospital.
Patients or Other Participants: A total of 40 patients with
ACLR (age ¼ 23.9 6 5.9 years, height ¼ 1.76 6 0.10 m, mass ¼
76.03 6 13.4 kg) and 17 healthy matched controls (age ¼ 28.4 6
5.9 years, height ¼ 1.70 6 0.10 m, mass ¼ 68.3 6 15.4 kg) were
recruited.
Main Outcome Measure(s): Knee-joint sagittal-plane kine-
matics were measured using 7 inertial measurement units pre-
operatively and 3 and 5 months postoperatively while
participants walked at slow, normal, and fast speeds.
Results: Preoperatively, compared with the contralateral
knee, the injured knee exhibited greater minimum flexion dur-
ing normal and fast walking (P  .008) and less knee flexion at
the first peak during fast walking (P ¼ .006). Statistical para-
metric mapping indicated differences throughout the gait cycle
at all speeds (P  .03). Compared with the control knee, the
injured knee had greater minimum flexion during normal and
slow walking (P  .03). At 3 months postoperatively, compared
with the contralateral knee, the injured knee exhibited greater
minimum flexion across all speeds (P  .005) and less knee
flexion at the first peak during fast walking (P , .001). Statisti-
cal parametric mapping indicated differences throughout the
gait cycle at all speeds (P  .03). Compared with the control
knee, the injured knee remained more flexed at the minimum
angle across all speeds (all, P , .001) and exhibited less knee
flexion at the first peak during slow walking (P ¼ .03). At
5 months postoperatively, differences between limbs were
reduced, with differences in minimum flexion at all speeds (P 
.03). Statistical parametric mapping differences were limited to
specific gait cycle portions during normal and fast walking (P 
.01). Compared with the control knee, the injured knee
remained more flexed at the minimum angle during slow and
normal walking (P  .005). Lastly, hip adaptations resolved,
and ankle asymmetries persisted during terminal stance.
Conclusion: Patients with ACLR demonstrated progres-
sive improvements in knee sagittal-plane kinematics, indicating
a recovery trend. However, the recovery was nonlinear across
different walking speeds.
Key Words: walking, kinematic analysis, lower limb
Key Points
• Patients with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) showed improved symmetry in knee-flexion angles at
3 and 5 months post-ACLR during various walking speeds.
• Asymmetries in knee, hip, and ankle kinematics were observed before ACLR, indicating altered movement patterns,
and persisted post-ACLR.
• The nonlinear recovery process across different walking speeds highlights the need for assessing and incorporating
varied walking speeds in rehabilitation protocols.
A
nterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction
(ACLR) often results in lasting kinematic asym-
metries while walking, reduced quality of life, and
increased risk of posttraumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA).1–3
Early gait assessment within the ﬁrst 6 months post-
ACLR is critical for guiding rehabilitation and reducing
long-term joint degeneration risks, as these asymmetries
can substantially affect knee function and potentially
accelerate PTOA development.2,4
Despite its clinical
importance, comprehensive biomechanical assessment
accounting for preoperative status, varying walking speeds,
and hip and ankle compensatory adaptations remains under-
explored. Moreover, traditional analyses focus primarily on
discrete time points of the gait cycle, limiting our under-
standing of continuous movement patterns in nonlaboratory
settings.
Journal of Athletic Training 823
Downloaded from https://nata.kglmeridian.com at 2026-07-03 via free access

--- PAGE 2 ---
The role of preoperative biomechanical status is often
underexplored, with few researchers providing preoperative
and postoperative assessments.5
This gap is important, as
preoperative biomechanics can inﬂuence postoperative
recovery outcomes.6–8
Speciﬁcally, Büttner et al demon-
strated that gait asymmetries are present preoperatively and
persist through recovery time points at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months
post-ACLR.9
Furthermore, Davis-Wilson et al observed
bilateral gait abnormalities in patients at 6 and 12 months
post-ACLR compared with uninjured controls, emphasizing
the need to assess recovery across multiple stages and walk-
ing speeds.10
Walking speed inﬂuences lower extremity biomechanics
post-ACLR, with faster speeds typically exacerbating biome-
chanical deﬁcits.11–13
This is particularly important, as daily
activities require walking at varying speeds—from slow
ambulation during routine tasks to fast walking when com-
muting or exercising. By assessing these speed-dependent
changes, clinicians can better understand how patients adapt
their movement strategies in real-world contexts and can
adjust rehabilitation interventions to improve performance
across all activity levels. However, authors of only a handful
of studies have assessed the inﬂuence of walking speed on
gait kinematics post-ACLR.11–13
Understanding how the rela-
tionship between walking speed and biomechanics changes
throughout rehabilitation might lead to better insight into
recovery patterns and real-world mobility demands.
Although knee kinematics is a primary concern post-
ACLR, assessing hip and ankle kinematics alongside it pro-
vides insight into compensatory strategies and overall
lower limb adaptation. Researchers have shown that
patients with ACLR display compensatory sagittal-plane
adaptations, speciﬁcally reduced hip ﬂexion and ankle dor-
siﬂexion, contributing to asymmetrical gait patterns.14–16
These adaptations may contribute to altered joint-loading
patterns throughout the kinetic chain.
Movement analysis is focused on speciﬁc gait events,
such as minimum and maximum points, providing impor-
tant snapshots of movement. However, continuous analysis
methods such as statistical parametric mapping (SPM) offer
a more comprehensive view of movement mechanics and
can be used alongside traditional discrete point analysis.17
Speciﬁcally, SPM addresses these limitations of discrete
analysis by examining continuous data, allowing the evalu-
ation of how joint angles change over time and identifying
differences or asymmetries that discrete analysis might
miss. For example, SPM analysis of walking has revealed
that knee sagittal-plane kinematic asymmetries post-ACLR
occur during extended portions of the stance phase rather
than just at discrete peak angles.11,18
Despite these advan-
tages, SPM remains underused in gait analysis, particularly
with inertial measurement unit (IMU) data in ACLR
populations.19
Traditional optoelectrical camera systems, while accurate,
are expensive and conﬁned to laboratory environments, reduc-
ing ecological validity.20,21
In contrast, wearable technologies
such as IMUs allow real-world kinematic data collection,
although normative values are needed to interpret differences
from optoelectrical data.22
Although no researchers have
directly linked IMU-based gait analysis to ACLR and PTOA
outcomes, IMU systems have shown promise in evaluating
gait deviations associated with osteoarthritis (OA). When
paired with SPM, wearable sensors have demonstrated the
ability to identify gait deviations associated with knee OA
that are characterized by asymmetries in ankle, knee, and hip
sagittal-plane kinematics during stance and swing phases.23
Greater asymmetries were associated with lower quality-
of-life scores measured using the Knee Injury and Osteoar-
thritis Outcome Score and Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis
Outcome Score, suggesting that IMU-based gait analysis can
provide meaningful insights into biomechanical asymmetries
and related quality-of-life measures.
The primary purpose of our study was to evaluate knee
sagittal-plane kinematic differences between injured and
contralateral limbs and healthy controls pre-ACLR and at 3
and 5 months post-ACLR using an IMU system during
slow, normal, and fast walking speeds. The secondary pur-
pose was to describe potential compensatory adaptations of
hip and ankle sagittal-plane kinematic differences at the
same time points. We hypothesized that patients with
ACLR would demonstrate differences in knee sagittal-
plane kinematics between the injured and contralateral
limbs and the injured and control limbs, with these differ-
ences decreasing but persisting by 5 months post-ALCR.
We also hypothesized that faster walking speeds would
magnify these between-limbs differences compared with
normal or slow walking speeds.
METHODS
Design
Data for this study were obtained from a randomized
clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT05001594), in
which the effect of local muscle vibration on the lower
limb kinematics of patients with ACLR was assessed. Fol-
lowing the framework of Lakens for sample-size justiﬁca-
tion in resource-constrained studies derived from previous
trials, we performed a sensitivity power analysis for a sam-
ple of 40 participants.24
This analysis revealed that, with an
a level of .05, our study had 80% power to detect effect
sizes (ESs) of 0.45, 90% power for ESs of 0.53, and
95% power for ESs of 0.58 in our between-limbs
comparisons.
In accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of
Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines, we con-
ducted a longitudinal observational study.25
The study
involved individuals scheduled for ACLR surgery, with
assessments conducted preoperatively and at 3 and
5 months postoperatively. Gait kinematics at 3 different
walking speeds were collected using an IMU motion-
capture system (Xsens Technologies, BV).
Participants
Participants were recruited from the Rambam Health
Care Campus Orthopaedic Department between 2020 and
2023 during their scheduled preoperative meetings. Gait
analysis was performed at 3 time points: preoperatively and
at 3- and 5-month postoperative follow-up visits.
We included male and female participants aged 18 to
40 years who were scheduled for ACLR using hamstrings,
bone-patellar tendon-bone, or quadriceps graft. The surger-
ies took place between 2020 and 2023 and were conducted
by a team of 5 experienced surgeons, each with 7 to
25 years of senior surgical experience.

--- PAGE 3 ---
Individuals were excluded if they had sustained multili-
gament injuries, substantial meniscus damage, or any other
concurrent injuries that altered the standard weight-bearing
protocol. We also excluded individuals who had a history
of previous knee surgery or fracture in either limb, known
neuropathies, active cancer, or inﬂammatory arthritis; had
received an injection for pain in the 6 months before the
study; or declined to participate. All participants followed a
standardized baseline rehabilitation protocol (Appendix
Table 1).
Volunteers matched by sex, weight, and height were
recruited for a healthy control group and underwent a similar
gait assessment protocol in a single testing session. The inclu-
sion criteria were male or female volunteers aged 18 to 40
with no self-reported lower limb or back pain in the 6 months
before the study. The exclusion criteria were a history of any
lower limb or back fractures, surgeries, known neuropathies,
active cancer, or inﬂammatory arthritis.
All participants provided written informed consent, and
the study was approved by the Rambam Health Care Cam-
pus Helsinki Committee (0089-21-RMB).
Gait Assessment
Each participant was ﬁtted with 7 IMUs (Xsens Awinda):
1 on each foot, 1 just below each knee, 1 on each midthigh,
and 1 on the pelvis. Data were collected, automatically pro-
cessed, and ﬁltered using proprietary software (MVN Ana-
lyze version 2023.0.0; Xsens) at a sampling rate of 100 Hz.
The system captures acceleration, angular velocity, and
magnetic ﬁeld data; exports them to a computer; and pro-
cesses them using biomechanical modeling algorithms and
proprietary software to compute joint angles, spatiotempo-
ral parameters, and segment orientations in 3 dimensions.26
This system was shown to be reliable compared with tradi-
tional motion capture.27
Before data collection, we performed a calibration
process to ensure accurate sensor alignment. Next, par-
ticipants were asked to walk across a 20-m corridor at 3
speeds: slow, normal, and fast. The following standard-
ized oral instructions were used for slow, normal, and
fast speeds, respectively: “Walk across the walkway at a
slow speed,” “Walk across the walkway at your normal
speed,” and “Walk as fast as possible.”28
Each speed was
repeated 3 times. The main discrete outcome was the
knee sagittal-plane angles, which comprised the ﬁrst
peak angle, deﬁned as the ﬁrst peak of knee ﬂexion dur-
ing the stance phase; the second peak angle, deﬁned as
the peak of knee ﬂexion occurring during the swing
phase; and the minimum ﬂexion angle, deﬁned as the
smallest knee-ﬂexion angle reached during the gait
cycle. The stance and swing phases were deﬁned as 0%
to 60% and 60% to 100% of the gait cycle, respectively.
The stance phase was subdivided into loading response
(0%–10%), midstance (10%–30%), terminal stance
(30%–50%), and preswing (50%–60%; Figure 1). The
secondary outcome was the minimum and maximum
sagittal-plane angles of the hip and ankle. All outcomes
were averaged and used for the ﬁnal analysis. Partici-
pants were asked to bring their own walking shoes and
wear the same shoes at each visit.
Statistical Analysis
Independent-samples t tests were used to compare con-
tinuous demographic variables, and v2
tests were used for
demographic categorical variables. Descriptive statistics
are presented as median (minimum, maximum). The
Figure 1. Knee sagittal-plane movement angle during the normalized gait cycle of healthy participants and commonly analyzed discrete
points. a
Point between the stance and swing phase.

--- PAGE 4 ---
median and interquartile range are reported for walking
speed for each walking condition grouped by time point.
The Wilcoxon signed rank test with the exact method was
used to compare the injured and contralateral limbs at each
time point, and the Mann-Whitney U test was used to com-
pare the injured limb and the left limb of the control group.
The Friedman test was used to assess differences between
walking speeds.
We used the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control
for multiple comparisons and false discovery rates. We
applied the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure separately for
each aim, ensuring that the control of the false discovery
rate was appropriate for each hypothesis and maintaining
statistical power without the results of one aim affecting
the other. The false discovery rate level was set at 0.1, bal-
ancing the need to detect true effects.29
Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess longi-
tudinal changes in the lower limbs. Each joint angle was
the independent variable, the time point was added as a
ﬁxed effect, and the participants with ACLR were added
as random effects. When differences were detected
between time points, the Bonferroni post hoc test was
used for pairwise comparisons between the different time
points. The analyses were carried out using SPSS Statis-
tics (version 29; IBM Corp) and Jamovi (version 2.4; The
Jamovi Project).
Before performing the SPM analysis, we normalized all
time-series data to 101 data points, representing 0% to
100% of the gait cycle. The data were interpolated to 101
evenly spaced points for each gait cycle using a linear inter-
polation function (scipy.interpolate.interp1d, SciPy version
1.15.0; SciPy). Discrete outcome measures were then
extracted from these normalized gait cycles, with the knee
sagittal-plane angles deﬁned as the ﬁrst peak angle, the sec-
ond peak angle, and the minimum ﬂexion angle. Next, 1-
dimensional SPM (spm1d version 3.7; Python Software
Foundation) was used to evaluate differences in the full
kinematic wave during walking. The spm1d nonparametric
paired-samples t test with 1000 permutations was used to
assess the limb differences. Mean 6 1 SD joint-angle tra-
jectory across participants is reported for SPM. The a level
for all tests was set at .05.
RESULTS
Participant Characteristics and Walking Speeds
Table 1 provides the descriptive data of the patients with
ACLR and control participants. Knee kinematics are pre-
sented in Table 2. We observed no differences in sex, age,
height, mass, and graft type between the participants who
attended the 5-month follow-up and those who were lost to
follow-up at 5 months post-ACLR (Appendix Table 2).
Figure 2 shows the difference in walking speeds at dif-
ferent time points. The results of the Friedman test showed
differences between slow, normal, and fast walking speeds
within each time point (presurgery: v2
2 ¼ 80.0, P , .001;
3 months: v2
2 ¼ 52.0, P ,.001; and 5 months: v2
2 ¼ 36.0,
P ,.001). When comparing the same speed categories across
time points, no differences were observed in slow (v2
2 ¼ 1.88,
P ¼ .39), normal (v2
2 ¼ 4.35, P ¼ .11), or fast (v2
2 ¼ 3.29,
P ¼.19) walking speeds, implying that speed was sustained
over the 3 time points.
Hip and ankle kinematics are detailed in Appendix
Tables 3 and 4, respectively.
Pre-ACLR Knee Kinematics
The discrete analysis showed that the injured limb exhib-
ited greater knee ﬂexion at the minimum ﬂexion angle
compared with the contralateral limb during normal (M ¼
1.78, SE ¼ 0.78; ES ¼ 0.48; P ¼.006) and fast (M ¼ 1.78,
SE ¼ 0.78; ES ¼ 0.57; P ¼.008) walking. The injured limb
showed less knee ﬂexion at the ﬁrst peak angle (M ¼
1.78, SE ¼ 0.88; ES ¼ 0.49; P ¼.006).
The SPM analysis revealed that the injured knee was
less ﬂexed than the contralateral knee across multiple por-
tions of the gait cycle (Table 3). During slow walking, dif-
ferences were observed from 12% to 54% of the gait cycle

(t ¼ 2.48, P ¼.001; Figure 3). During normal walking, dif-
ferences were observed from 24% to 48% of the cycle (t ¼
2.75, P ¼ .001; Figure 4). Differences were noted during
fast walking in 2 areas: 30% to 51% and 90% to 94% of
the gait cycle (t ¼ 2.79, P ¼ .002 and t ¼ 2.79, P ¼ .03,
respectively; Figure 5).
We observed that the injured knee of the patients with
ACLR was more ﬂexed at the minimum ﬂexion angle com-
pared with the knee of controls during slow (M ¼ 2.78;
ES ¼ 0.38; P ¼ .02) and normal (M ¼ 2.28; ES ¼ 0.37;
P ¼.03) walking.
3 Months Post-ACLR Knee Kinematics
The discrete analysis indicated that, compared with the
contralateral limb, the injured limb displayed greater knee
ﬂexion at the minimum ﬂexion angle (M ¼ 4.38, SE ¼
0.68; ES ¼ 0.96; P ,.001) and less knee ﬂexion at the sec-
ond peak angle (M ¼ 4.78, SE ¼ 0.88; ES ¼ 0.92; P ,
.001) during slow walking. The injured limb had greater
knee ﬂexion at the minimum ﬂexion angle (M ¼ 4.38,
SE ¼ 0.88; ES ¼ 0.98; P ,.001) and less knee ﬂexion at
the ﬁrst (M ¼ 5.28, SE ¼ 0.98; ES ¼ 0.86; P ,.001)
and second (M ¼ 2.28, SE ¼ 0.898; ES ¼ 0.60; P ¼
.005) peak angles during fast walking.
The SPM analysis showed multiple periods in which
the injured knee was less ﬂexed across all walking
speeds (Table 3). During slow walking, differences
between limbs occurred across 3 clusters of the gait
cycle: 0% to 3%, 19% to 61%, and 92% to 99% (t ¼
2.63, P ¼.03; t ¼ 2.62, P ¼.001; and t ¼ 2.62, P ¼.001,
respectively; Figure 3). We observed differences in nor-
mal walking from 26% to 59% and 90% to 99% of the
cycle (t ¼ 2.78, P ¼.001 for both; Figure 4). During fast
walking, differences were observed from 30% to 62%
and 90% to 97% of the gait cycle (t ¼ 2.86, P ¼.001 and
t ¼ 2.86, P ¼.008, respectively; Figure 5).
Compared with the control knee, the injured knee
remained more ﬂexed at the minimum ﬂexion angle at slow
(M ¼ 5.38; ES ¼ 0.78; P ,.001), normal (M ¼ 5.58; ES ¼
0.77; P ,.001), and fast (M ¼ 4.98; ES ¼ 0.71; P ,.001)
walking speeds. The knee was less ﬂexed at the ﬁrst peak
angle during slow walking (M ¼ 4.68; ES ¼ 0.39; P ¼.03).
5 Months Post-ACLR Knee Kinematics
Compared with the contralateral knee, the discrete analy-
sis showed that the injured knee was more ﬂexed at the
minimum ﬂexion angles during slow (M ¼ 1.58, SE ¼ 0.68;
ES ¼ 0.59; P ¼ .03) and normal (M ¼ 2.18, SE ¼ 0.78;
ES ¼ 0.76; P ¼ .003) walking speeds. The injured knee
was less ﬂexed at the ﬁrst peak angle during normal walk-
ing speed (M ¼ 1.98, SE ¼ 1.08; ES ¼ 0.53; P ¼.048),
but this ﬁnding was not different after correction.
Similarly, during fast walking, the injured knee was
more ﬂexed at the minimum ﬂexion angle (M ¼ 2.38, SE ¼
0.68; ES ¼ 0.86; P ,.001) and less ﬂexed at the ﬁrst peak
angle (M ¼ 5.18, SE ¼ 1.08; ES ¼ 0.83; P ,.001).
Figures 4 and 5 show that differences were limited to
93% to 95% of the gait cycle during normal walking (t ¼
2.86, P ¼.003) and 38% to 61% during fast walking (t ¼
2.83, P ¼.01). The injured knee remained less ﬂexed dur-
ing the loading phase during fast walking compared with

the contralateral knee, indicating that some asymmetries

the control knee, the injured knee was more ﬂexed at the

As seen in Table 4, changes were observed in knee kine-
matics from pre-ACLR to 3 months post-ACLR. At slow
walking speed, knee ﬂexion was increased for the mini-
mum angle (P ¼ .006). Similar patterns were observed at
normal (P ,.001) and fast (P ¼.006) walking speeds.
Associated Hip and Ankle Adaptations
After correction for multiple comparisons, differences
were observed at pre-ACLR in the ankle of the injured
limb that demonstrated increased plantarﬂexion (slow
speed, P ¼ .003) compared with the controls. No differ-
ences were noted between the injured and contralateral
limbs. By 3 months post-ACLR, the hip showed less ﬂex-
ion across all walking speeds (normal and slow, P ¼ .001
and fast, P ¼ .008) and less extension at normal walking
speed (P ¼.004) in the injured than contralateral limb. The

By 5 months post-ACLR, no differences were found in
the hip joints between limbs and between the injured and
control limbs. The ankle of the injured limb showed less
dorsiﬂexion and increased plantarﬂexion at slow walking
speed (P ,.05) compared with controls, but those ﬁndings
were not different after correction for multiple comparisons.
The results of the SPM analysis are available in Table 3, and
the discrete analysis is provided in Appendix Tables 3 to 6.
DISCUSSION
We assessed sagittal-plane kinematics during gait pre-
ACLR and post-ACLR using IMUs in a nonlaboratory
setting. Our primary ﬁndings indicated progressive improve-
ment in knee sagittal-plane kinematics symmetry post-
ACLR, particularly at 3 months post-ACLR, with compen-
satory adaptations observed in hip and ankle kinematics.
Few researchers have examined pre-ACLR and early post-
ACLR gait kinematics or the effect of walking speed on gait
asymmetries or have used SPM in this population.5,11,12,19,30
Pre-ACLR Knee Kinematics
The injured knee exhibited a more ﬂexed position during
most of the stance phase across all speeds and just before
the loading phase at fast speed. These results are consistent
with those of Gao and Zheng, who observed that patients
who were ,1 year since their ACL injury presented with a
less extended knee during the stance phase.31
The SPM anal-
ysis revealed that these asymmetries occurred predominantly
during midstance and terminal stance, highlighting how
weight-bearing activities speciﬁcally challenge movement
symmetry even before surgery. Increased knee ﬂexion dur-
ing stance may represent a protective mechanism to reduce
tibial translation and minimize ACL strain in the absence of
a functional ACL.32
The persistence of this pattern across
different walking speeds suggests it is a robust compensa-
tory strategy rather than a speed-dependent adaptation.
Three Months Post-ACLR Knee Kinematics
The discrete analysis found that, at 3 months post-
ACLR, participants demonstrated less knee ﬂexion at the
second peak during slow and normal walking speeds in
their injured than contralateral limb. During fast walking,
differences between limbs extended to include less ﬂexion
at the ﬁrst peak angle in the injured knee.
Whereas Williams et al reported smaller ﬁrst peak knee-
ﬂexion angle in the involved than uninvolved limb during
self-selected walking speeds (17.78 6 6.78 versus 20.98 6
4.78), we only observed this difference during fast walk-
ing.33
This discrepancy may be explained by walking speed
differences, as the self-selected speeds of their participants
were faster than those of ours, falling between our normal
Figure 3. One-dimensional statistical parametric mapping of the gait cycle for the anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and
contralateral limbs during slow walking at pre-ACLR and 3 and 5 months post-ACLR, respectively, for the, A–C, knee, D–F, hip, and G–I,
ankle. Solid lines indicate the mean joint-angle trajectory across participants, with shaded areas indicating 61 SD. Shaded gray boxes
indicate differences.

Downloaded from https://nata.kglmeridian.com at 2026-07-03 via free access

--- PAGE 8 ---
and fast conditions. Furthermore, Ferber et al found no dif-
ference in ﬁrst-peak knee-ﬂexion angle at a self-selected
walking speed but did not report on the actual walking
speed of the participants (control ¼ 16.18 6 2.18; ACLR ¼
19.88 6 5.48).34
The SPM analysis indicated that the injured knee was
more ﬂexed during most of stance and the beginning of the
swing phase across all walking speeds but had less peak
ﬂexion during the swing phase. Neal et al used SPM to
assess knee kinematics 3 months post-ACLR and reported
increased knee ﬂexion between 31% to 51% of the gait
cycle, consistent with our ﬁndings.18
On the contrary, they
found decreased knee ﬂexion between 6.5% and 20% of
the gait cycle. Notably, the self-selected speed in the study
by Neal et al was closer to our participants’ fast walking
speed, partially explaining this discrepancy.18
These ﬁndings reinforce the speed-dependent nature of
kinematic asymmetries post-ACLR, suggesting that move-
ment deﬁcits may be less apparent at slower walking
speeds but become more pronounced as task demands
increase. Furthermore, the late stance and terminal swing
asymmetries might highlight challenges in preparing for
the next gait cycle.
Five Months Post-ACLR Knee Kinematics
By 5 months post-ACLR, the injured limb improved, but
asymmetries persisted in terminal stance to preswing at fast
walking speed. This speed-dependent pattern demonstrates
how increasing task demands can reveal persistent move-
ment asymmetries that might not be apparent in less chal-
lenging walking.
Discrete analysis revealed that the knee was more ﬂexed
at the minimum ﬂexion angle and less ﬂexed at the ﬁrst
peak at normal and fast speeds compared with the contra-
lateral limb. These results differ from those of Georgoulis
et al, who assessed normal walking speed (1.28 m/s) and
found no differences at any discrete point of the gait cycle
at a walking speed similar to that in our study (1.26 m/s).35
One explanation is that Georgoulis et al compared 2 sepa-
rate groups (different participants for the pre-ACLR and
post-ACLR groups), whereas we performed within-subjects
comparisons.35
Neal et al assessed participants 6 months post-ACLR
and found differences between 5% to 18% and 36% to 48%
of the gait cycle.18
Similar to the 3-month comparison, the
self-selected speed was faster in their study than ours. The
differences in sample size, movement-capture systems, and
slightly different time points post-ACLR can further
explain the different results.
Although improvements during the ﬁrst 5 months post-
ACLR are evident, knee kinematics do not fully return to
preinjury levels even 1 year after surgery. Researchers have
shown that ACLR limbs have less peak knee ﬂexion com-
pared with control limbs, which could contribute to less-
than-optimal recovery.2
Furthermore, the persistence of

--- PAGE 9 ---
asymmetries primarily during midstance at faster speeds
might suggest that the neuromuscular system still struggles
with higher mechanical demands, such as excessive tibial
translation.36
Associated Hip and Ankle Adaptations
As a secondary ﬁnding, we observed several adaptations
in hip and ankle kinematics, possibly as a compensation
strategy for the changes in the knee joint. Pre-ACLR, hip
asymmetries were limited to midstance to terminal stance
during slow walking. Ankle asymmetries during this period
were evident in midstance to terminal stance when walking
at slow and normal speeds. At 3 months post-ACLR, hip
asymmetries persisted during midstance, terminal stance,
or preswing across all walking speeds. Similarly, ankle
asymmetries were observed in midstance and terminal
stance across all walking speeds. By 5 months post-ACLR,
hip asymmetries had resolved across all speeds, but ankle
asymmetries persisted during terminal stance at normal and
fast walking.
The resolution of hip asymmetries by 5 months com-
pared with the persistence of ankle asymmetries suggests
a joint-speciﬁc recovery pattern. These ﬁndings suggest

Clinical Implications
The comparison of our study with others highlights the
need for transparent, reproducible methodologies. Given
that some researchers did not report walking speeds and
others did not describe the exact oral cue given to their par-
ticipants, a heterogeneous comparison between studies is
hard to make.34,38
Our ﬁndings using IMU-based gait analysis aligned with
previous evidence supporting the clinical utility of wear-
able sensors in assessing knee pathologies. In a recent
study, Ghaffari et al demonstrated that IMU-derived gait
variables can be used to discriminate between individuals
with and those without knee OA.38
In addition, IMU mea-
surements have shown associations with patient-reported
outcomes and pain levels, suggesting their potential value
as objective markers of functional recovery.39,40
Whereas
researchers have primarily focused on primary knee OA,
we extended these ﬁndings to the ACLR population, dem-
onstrating that IMU-based gait analysis can capture subtle
biomechanical changes and potentially early identiﬁcation
of patients at risk for developing PTOA.
Our ﬁndings have important implications for post-ACLR
rehabilitation protocol design and implementation. The
nonlinear recovery patterns across walking speeds align
with those of previous studies in which increased asymme-
tries at faster speeds were shown.11,30,41
Our secondary ﬁnd-
ing of compensatory mechanisms, particularly evident at
higher speeds, may lead to excessive joint loading that
could increase the risk of early degenerative changes in
both the hip and ankle joints.41–44
Furthermore, different
walking speeds can reveal important insights: Slower walk-
ing speeds may highlight joint patterns similar to those
seen in OA, showing how patients with ACLR adapt their
gait.45
In addition, faster walking speeds place greater
demands on joint moments, muscle activation, and range of
motion.30
Limitations
We acknowledge some limitations in our study. Although
our sample size was determined by a previous trial rather
than an a priori power calculation, sensitivity power analyses
demonstrated our study had sufﬁcient power (80%) to detect
ESs of 0.45, aligning with the effects we observed (range,
0.48–0.98). We used a single-center design with a limited
follow-up period. However, the purpose of our study was to
describe the kinematic changes during the pre-ACLR and
early to middle stages of ACLR rehabilitation. We did not
account for different graft types and sex differences, possibly
introducing bias in our results. Furthermore, the participants
available for this study had varied times between their injury
and ACLR, which could have inﬂuenced their biomechanics
and ACLR outcomes. Next, multiple comparisons of knee-,
hip-, and ankle-joint kinematics might have increased type I
errors. However, we predeﬁned the knee-joint kinematic
analysis as the primary outcome of this study and adjusted
the results accordingly. In addition, the high dropout rate
may have introduced attrition bias, potentially linked to par-
ticipants missing predeﬁned check-up meetings with their
surgeon rather than the study itself. Lastly, although we
observed no differences in characteristics between the con-
trol and ACLR cohorts, the control participants were older
and shorter and weighed less, which could have inﬂuenced
their gait.
CONCLUSIONS
In our study, we highlighted several key ﬁndings regard-
ing gait recovery in patients with ACLR. We observed
improved symmetry in gait post-ACLR compared with the
contralateral limb and controls. However, these improve-
ments were inconsistent across different walking speeds,
suggesting that varying walking speeds may challenge
patients differently. Although hip and ankle adaptations
were noted, the primary focus on knee kinematics revealed
persistent asymmetries at faster walking speeds. These
ﬁndings underscore the importance of integrating varied
speed regimens in rehabilitation protocols to facilitate com-
prehensive recovery of knee function.

STEM Leadership Program (Dr Fischer) and the Israel Science

Appendix
Appendix Table 1. Baseline Rehabilitation Protocol
First week postoperatively
 Static quadriceps exercises in straightening.
 Walking with crutches or walker while applying partial weight on the operated leg.
 Wearing elastic socks and exercising calf muscles to avoid deep vein thrombosis.
7–14 d postoperatively
 Walking while fully stepping on the leg (can use crutches).
 Exercising to improve range of movement.
 After 2–3 wk, maximal recommended range of movement is 08–908.
Weeks 2–3
 Wall slides and heel slides exercises.
 Static vastus medialis obliquus exercises sitting down.
 Using rowing machine with minimal resistance and medium range of movement.
Week 4
 Bending exercises 08–1008 (avoid overstraightening).
 Static bicycles with low resistance.
 Up and down exercises with a low step.
 Squat exercises up to 458–608.
Week 8
 Step machine.
 Squat exercises.
Week 10
 Trampoline.
Week 12
 Achieving a range of movement of 08–1308 is recommended.
 Advancing in strengthening quadriceps and hamstrings.
3–6 mo
 Increasing gradual activity.
 Easy running starting in the 5th month.
 Changing directions, accelerations, deceleration, running in figure of 8.
 Preparing for a specific sport.
After 6 mo
 If everything is normal and the patient is confident to return to the specific sport, gradually exercise the specific sport.
7–9 mo
 Returning to the specific sport.
